Welcome back to your weekly roundup of AI legislation!

 

Housekeeping 

 

💬 NEW: Blog Posts - FPF published two new blog posts by Justine Gluck and Rafal Fryc discussing recent trends in the AI regulatory environment.

  • Voluntary AI Standards in US Regulations: Incentives or Obligations explores how states and courts are incorporating non-binding technical standards into legal requirements, nudging developers and deployers to adhere to established voluntary governance frameworks.
  • Chatbot Trends: The Chatbot Moment examines the growth of chatbot-related legislation in 2026, including two resources highlighting definitional patterns and mapping the six most common regulatory provisions. 

 

❗Help Us Improve Our Legislative Updates: The FPF U.S. Legislation team is gathering feedback on our weekly legislative updates. Please complete our short survey to share your preferences on content and frequency so we can better tailor these updates to your interests.

 

Highlights 

  • Blackburn Releases Federal AI Framework Draft: Sen. Blackburn (R-TN) introduced a discussion draft of the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act to establish a national AI framework, incorporating multiple previously introduced federal bills.
  • Work Group Agreement Reached on Colorado AI Act Amendments: A state work group reached agreement on a potential proposal to repeal and replace the Colorado AI Act, which would adjust scope to ADMT that materially influences consequential decisions, reducing governance requirements, and shifting toward post-adverse decision disclosures, human review, and AG-led rulemaking.
  • Tennessee Health Bill Passes Both Chambers: SB 1580 would prohibit the development/ deployment of an AI system that advertises that it is able to act as a qualified mental health professional.
  • 3 Bills Passed First Chamber: NH HB 1124 (right to compute) and SB 640 (health), PA SB 1090 (chatbots).

 

Stuff from the States

 

California - 

  • Employment - AB 2027: Introduced by Asm. Ward (D), this bill would prohibit collecting or sharing worker data for training AI systems that automate or replace jobs.
  • Health - AB 1979: Introduced by Asm. Bonta (D), this bill would expand California’s existing health privacy laws to cover AI and restrict the use of AI in clinical decision making. 
  • Transparency - SB 1130: Introduced by Sen. Reyes (D), this bill would prohibit unauthorized recording with wearable devices in business settings and require visible recording indicators.
  • Coalition Urges Pause on Chatbot Ballot Measure - A coalition of child safety and civil society organizations sent a letter urging OpenAI to withdraw its “Parents & Kids Safe AI Act” ballot initiative and to dissolve their 2026 ballot measure committee entirely, arguing it would weaken protections for children and limit accountability. The groups contend the proposal narrows definitions of harm, restricts enforcement and legal recourse, and could lock in inadequate standards through the ballot process. The letter calls instead for allowing the legislature to develop more comprehensive and adaptable AI safety protections for minors. However, this letter comes a month after OpenAI already stated their intent to pause their “Parents & Kids Safe AI Act” ballot campaign for 2026 in favor of passing legislation directly through the California Legislature this session. 

 

Colorado - 

  • Work Group Agreement Reached on Colorado AI Act Amendments: The Colorado AI Policy Work Group convened by Governor Polis has reached agreement on a potential policy framework to repeal and replace the Colorado AI Act. The proposed framework is expected to inform forthcoming legislation as it moves through the state legislative process. The framework includes:
    • Scope Shift: Narrows coverage to ADMT that materially influences consequential decisions, while clarifying and slightly expanding what qualifies as a consequential decision to include a broader range of impacts on access, eligibility.
    • Reduced Governance Requirements: Eliminates obligations such as annual impact assessments, risk management programs, and a general duty of care, and defers discrimination enforcement to existing laws.
    • Liability & Enforcement Changes: Limits developer liability to intended or marketed uses, requires allocation of fault between actors, includes three-year record retention requirements, and introduces a 90-day cure period for civil penalties.
    • AG Rulemaking: Directs the AG to adopt rules to implement post adverse ADMT disclosure requirements, including clarifying content and providing sector-specific guidance.
    • Other Updates: Delays the effective date to January 1, 2027 and expands certain exemptions (e.g., HIPAA).
  • Data-Driven Pricing Bill Passes Committee- HB 1210 (prohibit the use of surveillance data to set individualized prices or wages) heads for the House floor.

 

Connecticut - Omnibus AI Bill Passes out of Committee: SB 5, including provisions on chatbots, employment, GenAI, ADMT, frontier AI, and more, passed out of committee this week with a substitute. While the substitute text is not yet available, this bill previously would have implemented transparency and anti-bias measures in automated employment-related decision processes; require providers of AI companions to include protocols for detecting harmful content; and restrict minors’ interactions with those AI companions. The bill would have also required AI generated content to be clearly marked and detectable. 

 

Illinois - ADMT/ Gov Use- HB 3567: Introduced by Rep. Briel, this bill would prohibit state agencies and their contractors from using any ADS in functions related to public assistance benefits, or those that materially impact individual rights, civil liberties, safety, or welfare, unless there is continuous meaningful human review. The bill would also prohibit procurement of any ADS that would negatively affect existing employee rights, collective bargaining agreements, and employment conditions.

 

Minnesota - 

  • AI Safety/Transparency - SF 4509: Introduced by Sen. Quade (D), this bill would establish new safety, transparency, and disclosure requirements for AI developers. Requirements include published safety protocols, annual reviews, and disclosing incidents. Includes a private right of action.
  • Employment - SF 4573: Introduced by Sen. Quade (D), this bill would prohibit employers from using AI in employment decisions in ways that result in discrimination and requires employers to notify individuals when AI is used in such processes.

 

Missouri - Health Bills Pass Committee - HB 2318 and HB 2368 would both prohibit AI developers and deployers from advertising AI as a mental health professional.

 

New Hampshire - 

  • Right to Compute Bill Passes First Chamber - HB 1124: The bill would establish a right to compute, similar to enacted Montana SB 212.
  • Health Bill Passes First Chamber- SB 640: This bill would prohibit the use of AI to deliver any mental health service that requires a professional license unless the service is provided by a licensed practitioner.

 

New Jersey - 

  • Chatbot Bill Passes Committee - A 4732 would require companion chatbot providers to provide three hour human disclosure notifications to users. Unlike the majority of other chatbot bills pending in states, this bill would only set a disclosure requirement: requiring companion chatbot providers to provide three hour notifications to users. There is no safety protocol or minor specific requirements in the bill.
  • Transparency Bills Pass Committee- A 4733 would prohibit advertising gen AI as capable of practicing regulated professions. A 4730 would require clear notification to consumers when they are interacting with AI in commercial contexts. 
  • GenAI Bill with Implications for Chatbots Passes Committee- A 2767 would make it a crime to offer, sell, or distribute AI or automated interactive computer technology capable of performing or simulating sexual conduct directed at children. The bill provides an exception for AI technology that has safety features designed to stop a chatbot from simulating sexual conduct when it detects that a user is a child.
  • Data-Driven Pricing Bill Passes Committee - S 3612 would make it unlawful for personalized algorithmic pricing or surveillance pricing based on personal data to be used for the price of groceries or food, with exceptions for bona fide discounts.

 

Pennsylvania - Chatbot Bill Passes First Chamber: SB 1090 would establish new safeguards for minors interacting with AI companion chatbots. The bill would require disclosures that users are interacting with AI, including recurring notifications every three hours and prompts to take breaks. It would also mandate safeguards for minors against sexually explicit content and require a general disclosure stating that companion chatbots may not be suitable for minors. Similar to last year’s California SB 243 and current pending chatbot legislation, this bill would require the development of a safety protocol, including referring users to crisis service providers. The bill now heads to the House for consideration.

 

Tennessee - Health Bill Passes Both Chambers - SB 1580: This bill would prohibit the development or deployment of an AI system that advertises that it is able to act as a qualified mental health professional. The bill has not yet been transmitted to the Governor, who will have 10 days (except Sundays) to sign the bill once transmitted.

 

Vermont - Health Bill Passes Committee - H 816 (Illinois HB 1806-style bill). 

 

Upcoming Hearings

  • California - SB 867 (Chatbots), SB 1142 (GenAI), and SB 1146 (Health) are set to be heard April 6 in the Senate Privacy, Digital Technologies, and Consumer Protection Committee.
  • Illinois - HB 4711 (GenAI) and HB 3567 (ADMT/ Gov Use) are set to be heard March 20 in the House Cybersecurity Committee.
  • Missouri - HB 2032 (Chatbots) is set to be heard March 23 in the House Emerging Issues Committee.

 

Federal

 

Sen. Blackburn Introduces Discussion Draft for Federal AI Law: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) released a discussion draft of the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act, a proposal aimed at establishing a national AI framework and codifying elements of President Trump’s executive order on artificial intelligence. The proposal incorporates several previously introduced bills from other senators, including lawmakers such as Sen. Hawley (R-MO), Durbin (D-IL), Cantwell (D-WA), and others. Notably, the draft states that it does not preempt any generally applicable law that may address artificial intelligence (and does not include provisions broadly preempting state AI laws).

 

This release comes amid reports of broader congressional activity, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Commerce Chair Ted Cruz reportedly working with the White House on a separate national AI blueprint that could include federal preemption and be integrated into a larger legislative package. The draft includes the following:

 

  • AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act: Originally introduced by Sen. Hawley (R-MO), this bill would require certain companies and federal agencies to report quarterly to the Department of Labor on AI-related job impacts, including layoffs and job displacement. The bill would include an enforcement mechanism allowing both the Secretary of Labor and private parties to bring civil actions for violations.
  • Kids Online Safety Act: The draft also incorporates KOSA, requiring covered online platforms to implement tools and safeguards to protect users under 17 from online harms, as originally introduced by Sen. Blackburn (R-TN).
  • The GUARD Act: Originally introduced by Sen. Hawley (R-MO), this bill would require AI companies to implement a “reasonable age verification process,” ban AI companion chatbots for minors, and mandate disclosures that users are interacting with AI at the start of conversations and at 30-minute intervals, along with disclaimers that the system is not a substitute for professional advice. The bill would also establish criminal penalties for companies whose AI companions encourage suicide or solicit sexually explicit conduct from minors. The Attorney General would be granted enforcement authority, with state Attorneys General also authorized to bring civil actions on behalf of residents.
  • AI Risk Evaluation Act: Originally introduced by Sen. Hawley (R-MO), this bill would direct the Department of Energy (DOE) to establish an Advanced AI Evaluation Program to assess risks from frontier AI systems. The bill would apply to “advanced AI systems” above a compute threshold (10²⁶ FLOPs), requiring developers to participate in the program and provide information to DOE upon request. It would also prohibit deployment of covered systems until developers comply with evaluation requirements. The proposal reflects a frontier-model regulatory approach similar to California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act.
  • AI LEAD Act: Originally introduced by Sen. Durbin (D-IL) this bill would classify AI systems as products and create a federal cause of action for products liability claims against AI system developers. It would allow individuals and the Attorney General (and state AGs) to file suits against AI developers for defective design, failure to warn, express warranty, and unreasonably dangerous or defective product claims. Developers who “substantially modifies an AI system or intentionally misuses an AI system contrary to its intended use” may also be held liable.
  • COPIEDM Act: Originally introduced by Sen. Cantwell (D-WA), this bill would establish federal standards for AI content provenance, watermarking, and detection, requiring NIST-led guidelines and enabling FTC and state enforcement. It would also require AI providers to support attaching provenance information on generated content. 
  • Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government: This bill would codify the White House executive order, preventing woke AI in the federal government by only allowing agency heads to procure LLMs that are truthful in responding to user prompts seeking factual information and that are neutral and do not manipulate responses in favor of ideological biases.
  • Third-Party Audits for Political Bias: This bill incorporates a new provision that would aim to  require third-party audits for high-risk AI systems to prevent discrimination based on political affiliation.
  • Additional Provisions: The TRUMP AMERICA AI Act also incorporates the following: 
    • NO FAKES Act (originally introduced by Sen. Coons (D-DE)) would establish liability for the unauthorized use and distribution of digital replicas of individuals’ voices or likenesses.
    • Future of AI Innovation Act (based on a bill originally introduced by Sen. Cantwell (D-WA), but with amendments) that would promote public-private AI research partnerships, standards development, and national lab testbeds.
    • CREATE AI Act (originally introduced by Rep. Obernolte (R-CA)) would establish a national AI research resource to expand access to compute, data, and infrastructure.
    • SHIELD Act (based on a bill originally introduced by Rep. Levin (D-CA), but with amendments) would require data center operators to enter agreements with the Department of Energy to mitigate consumer rate impacts, or risk losing eligibility for federal incentives and assistance.
    • TRAIN Act (originally introduced by Sen. Welch (D-VT)) would enable copyright holders to use administrative subpoenas to obtain information on whether their works were used to train AI models.

 

Senator Introduces Bill on Military Use of AI: Introduced by Sen. Slotkin (D-MI), the AI Guardrails Act would establish guardrails on the Pentagon’s use of AI by codifying existing Department of Defense policies. The bill would prohibit the use of AI for autonomous lethal decision-making, domestic mass surveillance, and the launch or detonation of nuclear weapons.
